title: Particle Physics: The Standard Model and Its Open Questions
description: An upper-division course in particle physics for readers who have completed quantum mechanics (PHY 331 or equivalent). It follows the standard texts, Griffiths' Introduction to Elementary Particles, Thomson's Modern Particle Physics, and Halzen and Martin's Quarks and Leptons, and takes every measured value from the Particle Data Group's Review of Particle Physics. Starting from relativistic kinematics and symmetry, it builds quantum electrodynamics, quantum chromodynamics and the electroweak theory, then the Higgs mechanism and neutrino oscillation, always computing a number and comparing it with experiment. The final chapter treats what the Standard Model leaves unexplained, including the hierarchy (fine-tuning) problem and the cosmological constant problem, honestly as open questions.
prerequisites: Quantum mechanics at the level of PHY 331 (Griffiths and Schroeter): spin, addition of angular momenta, perturbation theory and Fermi's Golden Rule
Special relativity: Lorentz transformations and relativistic energy and momentum
Electromagnetism: Maxwell's equations, potentials and gauge transformations
Linear algebra with complex matrices, and comfort with multivariable calculus
objectives: Use four-vectors and Lorentz invariants in natural units to compute invariant masses, thresholds and decay kinematics.
Apply conservation laws and the discrete symmetries C, P and T to decide which reactions and decays are allowed.
Compute lowest-order decay rates and cross sections from Feynman rules, including electron-positron annihilation to muon pairs.
Explain the evidence for quarks, color, asymptotic freedom and confinement, and use the measured R ratio.
Describe charged and neutral weak currents, quark mixing (the CKM matrix) and electroweak unification, and use the measured Z width to count light neutrino species.
Explain how the Higgs mechanism gives mass to the W and Z bosons and the fermions, and interpret the 2012 ATLAS and CMS discovery data.
Compute neutrino oscillation probabilities and interpret atmospheric, solar, reactor and accelerator data.
State the hierarchy problem and the cosmological constant problem precisely, and separate measured facts from proposed solutions.

chapters.title: Relativistic Kinematics and the Particle Map
chapters.summary: The particles of the Standard Model, natural units, and the four-vector tools that turn detector measurements into masses, thresholds and lifetimes.
chapters.challenge: From the measured energies and directions of the two photons in a published Higgs-candidate event, compute their invariant mass and decide whether the event could come from a 125 GeV Higgs boson.

sections.title: A first map of the Standard Model
sections.summary: Quarks, leptons, force carriers and the Higgs boson, and the experiments that found each.

sections.title: Natural units and four-vectors
sections.summary: Setting ħ = c = 1, working in GeV and femtometers, and Lorentz-invariant products.

sections.title: Invariant mass, decays and thresholds
sections.summary: Two-body decays, collider versus fixed-target energies, and how a mass peak is found.

sections.title: Lifetimes, widths and cross sections
sections.summary: Time dilation of cosmic-ray muons, decay widths and branching ratios, and what a barn measures.

chapters.title: Symmetries and Conservation Laws
chapters.summary: How symmetries decide what can happen, from conserved quantum numbers to the gauge principle that generates every force.
chapters.challenge: Decide which of twelve proposed reactions and decays are allowed, name the conservation law each forbidden one breaks, and check two of your verdicts against branching-ratio limits in the Review of Particle Physics.

sections.title: Noether's theorem and conserved quantities
sections.summary: Energy, momentum, angular momentum, charge, baryon number and lepton number.

sections.title: Parity, charge conjugation and time reversal
sections.summary: The discrete symmetries, Wu's 1957 cobalt-60 experiment, and the CPT theorem.

sections.title: Isospin, SU(3) flavor and the quark model
sections.summary: The eightfold way, the predicted Omega-minus, and hadrons as combinations of quarks.

sections.title: The gauge principle
sections.summary: How demanding local phase symmetry produces the photon and electromagnetism.

chapters.title: Quantum Electrodynamics
chapters.summary: Feynman rules, the Dirac equation and a first complete calculation, tested against some of the most precise measurements in physics.
chapters.challenge: Calculate the lowest-order cross section for electron-positron annihilation to a muon pair at a center-of-mass energy of 10 GeV, convert it to nanobarns, and predict the angular distribution of the outgoing muons.

sections.title: Fermi's Golden Rule and Feynman diagrams
sections.summary: Decay rates and cross sections from amplitudes, and what a diagram does and does not depict.

sections.title: The Dirac equation and antiparticles
sections.summary: Spinors, the negative-energy solutions, the positron, and the electron's g = 2.

sections.title: Electron-positron annihilation to muon pairs
sections.summary: The first complete QED calculation: spin sums, traces and the 1 + cos²θ distribution.

sections.title: Running coupling and magnetic moments
sections.summary: Renormalization in plain terms, the fine-structure constant at different energies, and g - 2 for the electron and the muon.

chapters.title: Quarks, Gluons and the Strong Force
chapters.summary: The evidence for quarks and color, and how quantum chromodynamics explains both nearly free partons and permanently confined hadrons.
chapters.challenge: Use the measured R ratio plotted in the Review of Particle Physics to count the quark colors and to locate the charm and bottom thresholds.

sections.title: Seeing quarks: deep inelastic scattering
sections.summary: The SLAC electron-proton experiments, scaling, and partons.

sections.title: Color and the R ratio
sections.summary: Why the Delta-plus-plus needs color to obey the Pauli principle, and how electron-positron data count three colors.

sections.title: Asymptotic freedom and confinement
sections.summary: The running strong coupling, jets, and why no free quark has ever been seen.

sections.title: Inside the proton at the LHC
sections.summary: Parton distributions, and gluon fusion, the main way the LHC makes Higgs bosons.

chapters.title: The Weak Interaction and Electroweak Unification
chapters.summary: Charged and neutral weak currents, quark mixing and CP violation, and the unified electroweak theory tested at LEP.
chapters.challenge: Use the measured Z boson width and its partial widths from the Review of Particle Physics to show that there are three light neutrino species.

sections.title: Charged currents: beta decay, muon decay and parity violation
sections.summary: The V minus A structure, the Fermi constant from the muon lifetime, and left-handed neutrinos.

sections.title: Quark mixing, the CKM matrix and CP violation
sections.summary: Cabibbo's angle, three generations, and matter-antimatter differences in kaons and B mesons.

sections.title: Neutral currents and the W and Z bosons
sections.summary: Gargamelle's neutral currents in 1973 and the discovery of the W and Z at CERN in 1983.

sections.title: Electroweak unification
sections.summary: The Glashow-Weinberg-Salam theory, the weak mixing angle, and precision tests at LEP.

chapters.title: The Higgs Mechanism and the 125 GeV Boson
chapters.summary: Why the Standard Model needs a Higgs field, how the 2012 discovery was made, and what the boson's measured properties tell us.
chapters.challenge: From the signal and background event counts in a published diphoton mass window, estimate the local significance of the excess, then explain the look-elsewhere effect and why particle physicists require five sigma to claim a discovery.

sections.title: The mass problem
sections.summary: Why gauge symmetry forbids mass terms for the W and Z bosons and for the fermions.

sections.title: Spontaneous symmetry breaking and the Higgs mechanism
sections.summary: A field with a nonzero vacuum value, Goldstone bosons, and how the W and Z gain mass.

sections.title: Discovery at the LHC, 4 July 2012
sections.summary: ATLAS and CMS, the two-photon and four-lepton channels, and what five sigma means.

sections.title: Measuring the Higgs boson
sections.summary: Couplings that grow with mass, the width, and the self-coupling that is still to be measured.

chapters.title: Neutrinos: Oscillation and Mass
chapters.summary: How the missing solar neutrinos and the Super-Kamiokande atmospheric data showed that neutrinos change flavor and therefore have mass.
chapters.challenge: Using the two-flavor oscillation formula and mixing parameters from the Review of Particle Physics, predict the muon-neutrino survival probability for neutrinos arriving from above and from below through the Earth, and compare with the Super-Kamiokande zenith-angle deficit.

sections.title: The solar neutrino problem
sections.summary: Davis's Homestake experiment, the missing neutrinos, and SNO's resolution.

sections.title: Oscillation as a two-state quantum system
sections.summary: Flavor and mass states, the two-flavor formula, and the Super-Kamiokande result of 1998.

sections.title: Three flavors and the PMNS matrix
sections.summary: Mixing angles, mass splittings, reactor and accelerator experiments, and the unknown mass ordering.

sections.title: How heavy, and what kind?
sections.summary: Direct mass limits from beta decay, limits from cosmology, and the search for neutrinoless double beta decay.

chapters.title: Open Problems: Naturalness, Fine-Tuning and Beyond
chapters.summary: What the Standard Model leaves unexplained, stated precisely and treated honestly as open questions.
chapters.challenge: Write a two-page assessment of one proposed answer to the hierarchy problem: what it predicts, what the LHC has searched for, what has been excluded, and what evidence would change your mind.

sections.title: What the Standard Model does not explain
sections.summary: Dark matter, the matter-antimatter asymmetry, the origin of neutrino mass, and gravity.

sections.title: The hierarchy problem
sections.summary: Quantum corrections to the Higgs mass, what fine-tuning and naturalness mean, and why some physicists doubt naturalness as a guide.

sections.title: The cosmological constant problem
sections.summary: Estimates of vacuum energy versus the measured dark energy density, and why the mismatch is so large.

sections.title: Where the field goes next
sections.summary: Proposed answers from supersymmetry to anthropic reasoning, their experimental status, and the measurements that could decide.

preface:
On 4 July 2012, two experiments at CERN, ATLAS and CMS, announced a new particle with a mass of about 125 GeV. It had been predicted in 1964 as a consequence of an idea about how force-carrying particles can have mass. This book is about how predictions like that one are made, how they are tested, and how physicists decide that a small bump in a plot is real.

It is written for readers who have finished an upper-division course in quantum mechanics; our companion book, PHY 331, is the natural place to start. We follow the standard texts: Griffiths' Introduction to Elementary Particles for the pace, Thomson's Modern Particle Physics for the modern experiments, and Halzen and Martin's Quarks and Leptons where a calculation deserves to be done in full. Every measured number, whether a mass, a lifetime or a mixing angle, comes from the Particle Data Group's Review of Particle Physics with its uncertainty, because a value without an error bar is not a measurement.

The method is the same in every chapter: find the symmetry, turn it into Feynman rules, calculate a number, and compare it with what a detector saw. Four results keep returning. The 125 GeV Higgs boson first appears as an invariant-mass peak in Chapter 1. Electron-positron annihilation is the cleanest laboratory we have for QED, for quarks and gluons, and for the Z boson. The muon takes us from time dilation in cosmic rays to the strength of the weak force. Neutrino oscillation, established by Super-Kamiokande in 1998, was the first clear sign that the Standard Model as first written is incomplete.

The last chapter is about what we do not know. The Standard Model does not explain dark matter, the excess of matter over antimatter, or why the Higgs boson is as light as it is, and simple estimates of the energy of empty space disagree with observation by an enormous factor. These are the fine-tuning problems. I will tell you exactly what each one is, what has been proposed, what the LHC has and has not found, and where careful physicists disagree.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a particle physicist who has worked through the calculations and also read the event displays: each force is introduced by its symmetry, turned into Feynman rules, computed to a number, and checked against a measured value from the Review of Particle Physics. Griffiths sets the level and pace, Thomson supplies the modern experiments and their data, and Halzen and Martin supply the fuller calculations; the discovery papers are read as primary sources.
bible.promise: By the last page you will compute decay rates and cross sections from Feynman rules, read a discovery plot and judge its significance, explain how the Higgs mechanism and neutrino oscillation work, and state precisely what the Standard Model does not explain.
threads: Symmetry decides the forces: each interaction comes from a gauge symmetry, and a broken symmetry explains mass.
Calculate, then compare: every diagram becomes a number that a detector can check.
How we know: every measured value comes from the Review of Particle Physics with its uncertainty, and every discovery is tied to the experiment and the data that made it.
The Standard Model is extraordinarily successful and known to be incomplete; we say exactly where it fails and where it only seems unnatural.
Built on quantum mechanics (PHY 331): spin, angular momentum, two-state systems, perturbation theory and identical particles are used, not re-taught.

runningExamples.name: The 125 GeV Higgs boson (ATLAS and CMS, 2012)
runningExamples.use: An invariant-mass peak in Chapter 1, made mostly by gluon fusion in Chapter 4, the consequence of symmetry breaking and the subject of Chapter 6, and the center of the hierarchy problem in Chapter 8.

runningExamples.name: Electron-positron annihilation
runningExamples.use: The cleanest laboratory: kinematics in Chapter 1, the first full QED calculation in Chapter 3, the R ratio and jets in Chapter 4, and the Z lineshape at LEP in Chapter 5.

runningExamples.name: The muon
runningExamples.use: Time dilation of cosmic-ray muons in Chapter 1, lepton number in Chapter 2, g - 2 in Chapter 3, the Fermi constant from its lifetime in Chapter 5, and muon-neutrino disappearance in Chapter 7.

runningExamples.name: Neutrino oscillation (Super-Kamiokande, 1998)
runningExamples.use: Left-handed neutrinos and helicity in Chapters 3 and 5, a two-state quantum system (PHY 331 Chapter 3) over thousands of kilometers in Chapter 7, and the open question of where neutrino mass comes from in Chapter 8.

conventions: Natural units (ħ = c = 1) from Chapter 1 onward; convert final answers to SI units with ħc = 197.3 MeV fm and show the conversion.

Every measured value (masses, widths, lifetimes, couplings, mixing parameters) comes from the 2026 Review of Particle Physics, quoted with its uncertainty and the listing it comes from; never quote a measured value from memory or a secondary source. If a value is taken from the 2024 edition, say so.
Metric signature (+, -, -, -) and Griffiths' notation; state it when Thomson or Halzen and Martin use a different normalization or convention.
Feynman diagrams are drawn with time running from left to right, and the caption says so.
Report significances as local or global, and use the experiments' own language: 'evidence' at three sigma, 'observation' at five sigma.
Label speculative ideas (supersymmetry, extra dimensions, the multiverse) as proposals, with their experimental status and the date of that status.
Refer back to PHY 331 by chapter when using quantum mechanics (for example, Fermi's Golden Rule, PHY 331 Chapter 7).

canon.role: The main text: level, pace and order of topics, from kinematics and symmetries through QED, QCD, weak interactions, neutrino oscillations and the Higgs mechanism.

canon.cite: Thomson, M. (2013). Modern particle physics. Cambridge University Press.
canon.role: Companion text for the experimental side: modern data from LEP, the B factories, neutrino experiments and the LHC, and complete worked calculations.

canon.role: Classic companion for fuller calculations in QED, partons and QCD, and the Weinberg-Salam model.

canon.role: The reference for every measured value (masses, lifetimes, couplings, mixing angles). Always take numbers from the newest edition at pdg.lbl.gov and cite the edition used.

canon.role: Primary source for the Higgs discovery (Chapters 1 and 6).

canon.role: Primary source for the Higgs discovery (Chapters 1 and 6), read side by side with the ATLAS paper.

canon.role: Prerequisite text of the companion course PHY 331: the spin, angular momentum, perturbation theory and Golden Rule this book assumes.

bible.care: Chapter 8 deals with open problems; keep measurement, theory and speculation clearly apart. The hierarchy (naturalness, fine-tuning) problem and the cosmological constant problem are genuine open questions: state what is measured (the Higgs mass, the dark energy density), what is a theoretical expectation and on what assumptions it rests, and why physicists disagree about whether naturalness is a reliable guide. Do not claim that the LHC has disproved supersymmetry or that naturalness proves new physics must exist; report the excluded mass ranges as the experiments state them, with dates. 'Fine-tuning' here is a technical term about sensitive cancellations in a theory; it is not, by itself, an argument for design or for a multiverse. Present anthropic reasoning as one proposal that physicists debate, fairly and without endorsing or mocking it. Mention the nickname 'God particle' only to explain where it came from and why physicists avoid it.
